# Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS)  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

### 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) replaces the existing study-room reservation tool across three university libraries. Students and staff must be able to search rooms and equipment, create and manage reservations, and receive reminders. Library staff must manage room information, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms display the current and next reservation.

The system integrates with four external or legacy systems:

- The university identity provider through SAML.
- Facilities calendar data through iCal feeds.
- A read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database.
- Email/push notification providers.

The most important constraints are 99.5% monthly availability during opening hours, availability-search p95 latency below 400 ms for 2,000 concurrent users, authenticated actions and audited staff activity, configuration-only onboarding of new campuses, database- and network-independent testing of reservation rules, and deployment or rollback by a two-person team within ten minutes.

The design covers the first release of the CLRS application and its supporting deployment, testing and operational practices. It does not replace the university identity provider, facilities calendar, notification providers or legacy inventory database.

# Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS)  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

### 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It supports students and staff across three libraries. Students can search for rooms and equipment, create or modify reservations, cancel reservations, and receive reminders. Library staff can manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. A kiosk outside each room displays the current and next reservation.

CLRS must integrate with:

- The university’s SAML identity provider;
- Facilities calendar iCal feeds;
- A read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database;
- Email and/or push notification infrastructure.

The design must satisfy the functional requirements FR-1 to FR-6 and quality requirements QR-1 to QR-6. The most important architectural concerns are reliable conflict-free reservation rules, fast availability searches, graceful kiosk degradation, security and auditability, configuration-based onboarding of new campuses, testability, and deployment by a two-person team.

The proposed architecture is a **modular monolith using hexagonal architecture**. The system is deployed as one application, but its business capabilities are separated into modules and its domain logic is isolated behind ports and adapters.

Students and staff search for rooms and equipment, create or modify reservations, and cancel bookings. Library staff manage rooms, opening hours, block bookings and utilisation reports. CLRS integrates with:

- The university identity provider through SAML.
- Facilities calendars through iCal feeds.
- A read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database.
- Email and push-notification providers.

The first release must support room availability search, reservation lifecycle operations, staff block bookings, kiosk schedules, reminders and monthly utilisation reports. Important quality constraints include 99.5% monthly availability during opening hours, availability-search p95 latency below 400 ms for 2,000 concurrent users, authenticated actions, audited staff operations, configuration-only onboarding of new campuses, database-independent reservation-rule testing, and deployment or rollback by a two-person team within ten minutes.

This document selects an architectural style, describes the resulting structure, and defines testing, delivery, observability, risks and open questions for implementation.
